lesson.title: Singular vs Plural Possessions
lesson.subtitle: mi amigo vs mis amigos, su libro vs sus libros, nuestro/nuestra

hook.title: One Owner, Many Possessions
hook.content: In English, 'my book' and 'my books' use the exact same 'my'. In Spanish, if you own two books or two keys, the possessive MUST put on its plural -s: mis libros, tus llaves, sus amigos!

pattern.title: Why 'Los Padres' Means 'The Parents'
pattern.content: In Spanish, the masculine plural of family words covers mixed-gender pairs: el padre ('the father') + la madre ('the mother') = mis padres ('my parents'); el hermano + la hermana = mis hermanos ('my brothers and sisters / siblings')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: mi amigo, mis amigos, tu llave, tus llaves, nuestra casa, mis padres
exercises.meaning: my friend, my friends, your key, your keys, our house (feminine), my parents
exercises.explanation: Possessives pluralize whenever the noun they modify is plural.

exercises.prompt: How does Spanish say 'our books' (masculine plural)?
exercises.explanation: el libro is masculine plural (los libros), so nuestro becomes nuestros.

exercises.idea: say that your parents live in Madrid
cues: live (3rd person plural of vivir) → viven

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.

summary.outcome: Pluralize mi/tu/su to mis/tus/sus and match nuestro/a/os/as to any noun.

use_example.german: Mis padres están en nuestra casa con mis amigos.
use_example.english: My parents are in our house with my friends.

summary.takeaway: Plural noun = plural possessive (mis, tus, sus, nuestros, nuestras).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1402] Disambiguating su): see why 'su' covers five English words and how Spanish makes it crystal clear.

twist.explanation: ¿Dónde están tus llaves? uses plural están + tus llaves.

mi.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the possession
mi.context_phrase: Es mi amigo y ellos son mis amigos.
mi.context_translation: He is my friend and they are my friends.
mi.etymology_derivation: Unstressed mi (no accent) means 'my'; accented mí (after a preposition: para mí) means 'me'!

tu_poss.shift_rule: No accent on possessive tu ('your') vs. accented tú ('you')

su.english_meaning: his, her, its, your (usted), their (plural: sus)
su.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the thing owned (su / sus)
su.context_translation: María is looking for her brother.
su.etymology_derivation: Only changes for singular (su libro) vs. plural (sus libros) — never for gender!

nuestro.english_meaning: our (agrees in gender and number: nuestro/a/os/as)
nuestro.etymology_derivation: Unlike mi/tu/su, nuestro agrees in both gender and number: nuestro padre, nuestra madre.

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

padre.etymology_derivation: Plural los padres means 'the parents' (mother and father together).

llave.etymology_derivation: Latin clāvis ('key') gives English 'clavicle' (little key bone) and Spanish llave.
